evidence.reference_title: Spinocerebellar [corrected] Ataxia Type 6: Molecular Mechanisms and Calcium Channel Genetics.
evidence.snippet: Genetically, SCA6 is caused by expansion of a trinucleotide CAG repeat in the last exon of longest isoform CACNA1A gene on chromosome 19p13.1-p13.2.

nodes.description: The SCA6 CAG expansion lengthens a polyglutamine tract in the C-terminal region encoded by CACNA1A. Mutant Cav2.1 accumulates in Purkinje cells and produces cytoplasmic aggregates. Current knock-in evidence supports misfolded-protein/ER stress, an initially protective HSP90-dependent unfolded-protein response, and age-related loss of that compensation, followed by store-operated calcium current and Purkinje-cell membrane hyperexcitability. The contribution of altered intrinsic Cav2.1 ion flux remains debated and is not modeled as a directional loss of calcium transport.

nodes.description: In the original SCA26 pedigree, the segregating EEF2 p.Pro596His substitution affects a conserved domain required to maintain the reading frame during translation. The yeast-equivalent variant increases programmed -1 ribosomal frameshift read-through and sensitizes cells to unfolded-protein stress. Because evidence is centered on one family and functional model systems, this mechanism remains provisional pending independent human replication.

nodes.description: No established disease-modifying therapy exists for the canonical ADCA-III subtypes. Management uses physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy and home adaptation, speech and language therapy for dysarthria and dysphagia, and mobility or communication aids as needed. Subtype-specific experimental drugs should be represented as clinical trials rather than routine treatment.

evidence.reference_title: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 26 maps to chromosome 19p13.3 adjacent to SCA6.
evidence.snippet: All affected family members had a slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, with an age of onset range from 26 to 60 years.

nodes.description: The canonical ADCA-III subtypes converge clinically on predominant cerebellar cortical dysfunction and atrophy. Purkinje cells are the best established vulnerable population in SCA5, SCA6, SCA11, and SCA31; SCA26 and SCA30 show cerebellum-confined atrophy in the defining families. Purkinje-cell firing dysfunction can precede overt cell loss, so the common node represents both functional failure and later degeneration rather than requiring histologic cell loss in every subtype.

evidence.snippet: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (SCA6) is one of the eight neurodegenerative diseases caused by a tri-nucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion coding polyglutamine (CAG repeat/polyglutamine diseases) and is characterized by late onset autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia and predominant loss of cerebellar Purkinje cells.

nodes.description: The pathogenic SCA31 insertion contains a long (TGGAA)n tract in an intron shared by oppositely transcribed BEAN1 and TK2. The BEAN1-direction (UGGAA)n transcript forms nuclear RNA foci in Purkinje cells, binds serine/arginine-rich splicing factors, and is toxic in cultured-cell systems, supporting repeat-RNA toxicity and disturbed RNA processing.

evidence.reference_title: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 5.
evidence.snippet: Ikeda et al. (2006) discovered that β-III spectrin (SPTBN2) mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 5 (SCA5) in the American kindred and two additional independently reported SCA5 families.

nodes.description: In SCA5, mutant beta-III spectrin disrupts organization of the Purkinje-cell dendritic membrane. Beta-III spectrin normally stabilizes and positions postsynaptic proteins including EAAT4 and mGluR1alpha. Mutant SPTBN2 causes mGluR1alpha mislocalization, reduced mGluR1 signaling, and impaired synaptic plasticity, creating a cell-selective route to cerebellar dysfunction.

evidence.reference_title: Mutant β-III spectrin causes mGluR1α mislocalization and functional deficits in a mouse model of spinocerebellar ataxia type 5.
evidence.snippet: These results indicate that mutant β-III spectrin causes mislocalization and dysfunction of mGluR1α at dendritic spines and connects SCA5 with other disorders involving glutamatergic dysfunction and synaptic plasticity abnormalities.

evidence.reference_title: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 11-associated alleles of Ttbk2 dominantly interfere with ciliogenesis and cilium stability.
evidence.snippet: SCA11 is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Serine/Threonine kinase Tau tubulin kinase 2 (TTBK2) that result in premature truncations of the protein.

nodes.description: SCA11-associated frameshift variants truncate TTBK2 after its kinase domain. In knock-in and allelic-series experiments, the truncated protein interferes with full-length TTBK2, decreases cilium formation and stability, and disrupts cilium-dependent Sonic hedgehog signaling. This provides a strong model-system mechanism, although the exact adult human Purkinje-neuron path from ciliary failure to degeneration remains incomplete.

evidence.reference_title: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 11-associated alleles of Ttbk2 dominantly interfere with ciliogenesis and cilium stability.
evidence.snippet: In this work, we present evidence that SCA11-associated mutations are dominant negative alleles and that the resulting truncated protein (TTBK2SCA11) interferes with the function of full length TTBK2 in mediating ciliogenesis.
